topic: Mastering the Cross Product: From 2D intuition to 3D mechanics

sections.title: Conceptual Foundations (Prerequisites)
sections.content: Define vectors as directed line segments. Introduce the 'Right-Hand Rule' as the fundamental constraint for 3D orientation. Briefly explain that while the dot product yields a scalar (projection), the cross product generates a new vector perpendicular to the original plane.
sections.example: Visualizing a clock hand: The vector points towards the center of the clock, representing the axis of rotation.

sections.title: 2D 'Cross Product' as Oriented Area
sections.content: Explain the 2D cross product (determinant of a 2x2 matrix). Crucially, frame this as the 'signed area' of a parallelogram formed by two vectors. If the sequence is counter-clockwise, the result is positive; clockwise results in negative.
sections.example: A robot arm in 2D space moving between vectors (1,0) and (0,1); the area is 1, representing the space swept by the arm.

sections.title: The 3D Cross Product Mechanics
sections.content: Extend to 3D using the determinant expansion (i, j, k unit vectors). Emphasize that the magnitude |a × b| = |a||b|sin(θ). Use a 3D animation showing the resulting vector 'growing' out of the plane as the angle between the two base vectors changes.
sections.example: A spinning propeller blade: The two vectors are the blade length and the spin force; the cross product represents the resulting thrust vector pushing the aircraft forward.

sections.title: Geometric Interpretations & Applications
sections.content: Summarize the utility: 1. Finding a normal vector to a surface (essential for computer graphics lighting). 2. Calculating torque in physics. Reinforce that if the cross product is zero, vectors are collinear.
sections.example: A monkey turning a wrench: The force applied to the handle (vector 1) at a distance from the bolt (vector 2) creates a torque vector (cross product) that drives the bolt into the wall.
